query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for plasma-facing applications in fusion reactors, what single intervention could improve radiation tolerance while preserving mechanical integrity and engineering practicality? Formulate one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the proposed mechanism, predicts a measurable improvement over the unmodified baseline, defines the conditions under which the effect should hold, cites prior evidence supporting the causal rationale, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) produced by additive manufacturing, the deliberate introduction of a small fraction of titanium (≈2–5 at.%) that forms coherent TiC nanoprecipitates (through available carbon during processing) will act as defect sinks to reduce He bubble growth during irradiation, thereby enhancing radiation tolerance without degrading mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-based RHEA (e.g., a W–Ta–Cr–V system) produced via additive manufacturing with a largely homogeneous BCC microstructure and no deliberate second-phase precipitates.
generation.intervention: Add a modest amount (≈2–5 at.%) of Ti to the alloy composition such that during processing, in the presence of trace carbon, finely dispersed coherent TiC nanoprecipitates form in situ.
generation.conditions: Irradiate the as-fabricated alloy at reactor-relevant conditions (e.g., helium ion irradiation at approximately 200 keV, 900°C, and fluences typical for plasma-facing applications) and compare with an otherwise identical baseline alloy without Ti addition.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent TiC nanoprecipitates evenly dispersed in the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates provide sites for defect recombination and serve as sinks for helium atoms, thereby limiting the growth and coalescence of He bubbles. At the same time, their coherent nature minimizes stress concentrations and contributes to dispersion strengthening, helping to preserve or even enhance the alloy’s mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Ti–doped RHEA will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the average size of He bubbles and a lower irradiation-induced hardening fraction, while maintaining similar or improved tensile strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The unmodified tungsten-based RHEA produced without Ti addition, which under similar irradiation conditions shows larger He bubble sizes and greater radiation-induced hardening.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under the specific additive manufacturing processing route that allows for in situ formation of coherent nanoprecipitates and at the tested irradiation conditions. Variations in Ti content, carbon availability, or processing parameters could alter the effectiveness of the intervention.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti content and precise processing conditions needed to reliably form the desired coherent TiC nanoprecipitates are not yet defined and will require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of tungsten-based RHEA samples using the same additive manufacturing procedure: one set with a 2–5 at.% Ti addition (targeting in situ TiC nanoprecipitate formation) and one control set without Ti. Subject both sets to helium ion irradiation at ~200 keV and ~900°C with a controlled fluence typical of plasma-facing applications. After irradiation, perform microstructural characterization via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to measure He bubble size and density and conduct mechanical testing (e.g., nanoindentation and tensile tests) to evaluate hardness, yield strength, and ductility.
measurements: He bubble size and density via TEM
Irradiation-induced hardness and tensile properties (yield strength and elongation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in He bubble size/density and/or if their mechanical integrity (tensile strength/ductility) is degraded relative to the control samples, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The presence of metastable phases has also been found to deteriorate the mechanical properties of W-Ti and W-V (to a lesser extent than that found in W-Ti) binary alloys. The difficulty associated with obtaining a perfect solid solution in W-V, the grain growth and the reduced elongation (or ductility) associated with W-Mo alloys also hinder the utilization of W-based binary alloys in harsh service environments. The drawbacks of W alloys play a role in diverting researchers’ attention towards high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for the future development of W-rich materials for plasma-facing applications.

While pure W may have the most ideal combination of the He bubble size and density of the materials studied here, there are significant concerns for the usage of W in a fission or fusion reactor, including its ductile–brittle transition temperature, recrystallization, and the ability to fabricate complex components. The performance of additively manufactured RHEAs in other areas relevant for reactors, including fracture properties and recrystallization performance, must be explored further. Future studies will elucidate the mechanical performance and high-temperature performance of the RHEAs studied here, including the potential for self-healing. Helium irradiation and He bubble formation and accumulation is just one aspect of materials design that should motivate materials choices for future reactors. In this work, we show that compositionally complex (spanning two, three, and four-component alloys) can be developed with AM processing routes.
